stories.headline: Nepal floods: 4 at hydropower tunnel among 108 Indians rescued; toll 682
stories.title: Nepal floods: 4 at hydropower tunnel among 108 Indians rescued; toll 682
stories.summary: Nepal's Bhote Koshi-Trishuli disaster death toll reached 675, with 2,426 people still missing. Rescuers searched mud-filled valleys and tunnels three days after the catastrophic flood occurred. Chinese authorities reported seven deaths and 554 missing at Gyirong port across the border. Indian nationals unaccounted for in Nepal were revised down to 287. India sent relief and worked to bring back citizens stranded on the Chinese side.

stories.headline: Mirwaiz urges J&K political parties to strive for restoration of statehood, condemns threat to Kashmiri Pandits
stories.title: Mirwaiz urges J&K political parties to strive for restoration of statehood, condemns threat to Kashmiri Pandits
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 29: Kashmir chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq on Saturday asserted that political parties from Jammu and Kashmir should make efforts for restoration of statehood and Article 370, saying it is their moral responsibility to raise their voice for the rights of people. “Our rights were snatched away by force. Our statehood was abolished, we were made a Union territory. The government should uphold the promises made to people prior to the elections,” Farooq told reporters here. The preacher also termed alleged threats to Kashmiri Pandits residing in the Valley “deeply unfortunate”. “We have consistently reiterated that Kashmiri Pandits are an integral part of our society, history, culture, and our future. They are not outsiders, they belong here. We have always advocated for their return and will continue our efforts, as should the government,” he asserted. Lashing out at the NC-led government, the Mirwaiz accused it of losing sight of its priorities. They have been unable to instill confidence in people regarding their “snatched” rights, the splitting of Jammu and Kashmir, and the “complete disregard” for constitutional commitments, he added. He said the Centre had essentially revoked all the promises made to Jammu and Kashmir since 1947. “They revoked all constitutional guarantees. So, it is the moral responsibility of mainstream political parties to stand up for these issues. They must raise their voice for restoration of rights of the people of Jammu and Kashmir and present a unified voice in this regard,” he added. On Srinagar MP Ruhullah Mehdi’s decision to quit the Lok Sabha and the National Conference (NC), the Mirwaiz hailed the parliamentarian as a staunch voice committed to raising people’s issues, and urged all organisations and parties of Jammu and Kashmir to follow suit. “They must stand by these constitutional guarantees, the commitments they made to people, their manifesto, and their election plank,” he said. He also criticised the government over hike in electricity tariff. “The government must recognise that Jammu and Kashmir’s economy is already going through a very fragile phase. Common, low-income citizens are in no position to endure escalating power tariffs. The administration should have deferred this increase,” he said. The Mirwaiz expressed solidarity with the victims of the Nepal tragedy and their families, asserting that the flash flood disaster should serve as a warning for Jammu and Kashmir. “We also reside in this Himalayan region. Over the past couple of years, we have seen changing weather patterns and climatic shifts driven by global warming. God has blessed Kashmir with immense natural beauty. Protecting this is our foremost responsibility,” he said. He said while people want development, tourism and infrastructure, “it cannot come at the cost of our ecology and environment”. Farooq said human interference with the ecosystem is largely responsible for weather vagaries and natural disasters. “While we will hold the administration accountable, we must also introspect. “Unplanned and unregulated construction continues unchecked across tourist destinations and fragile hilly terrains like Pahalgam. If this persists, we are heading toward an ecological disaster. Authorities and policy experts must formulate a well-structured roadmap to safeguard this Himalayan belt,” he said.

stories.headline: Is Kashmir going Nepal way? Himalayan extremes set alarm bells ringing
stories.title: Is Kashmir going Nepal way? Himalayan extremes set alarm bells ringing
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 29: The devastation in Nepal has sent a chilling warning across Jammu and Kashmir: when a warming climate meets fragile mountain terrain and unchecked human intervention, an extreme weather event can rapidly turn into a catastrophe. For J&K, the question is no longer whether climate change is altering the Himalayan environment. It is whether the Valley is adequately prepared for the increasingly erratic and intense weather events being witnessed across the region. Nepal recently witnessed a devastating flash flood in the Lhende Khola area near the Nepal-Tibet border after an ice-and-rock avalanche entered the river system. The torrent swept away homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure, leaving a trail of destruction and triggering a major rescue operation. The disaster has once again drawn attention to the growing vulnerability of Himalayan communities to glacial, geological and weather-related hazards. Kashmir, meanwhile, has been experiencing its own alarming pattern. J&K has witnessed 40 cloudbursts, flash floods and landslides this summer, with incidents reported from Kishtwar, Doda, Ramban, Pahalgam, Shopian, Kulgam, Bandipora and Kupwara. In several cases, streams that normally remain relatively calm have transformed into torrents within minutes, damaging roads, bridges, homes and agricultural land. Climate expert Dr Tauseef Ahmad Bhat said the developments in Nepal should be viewed as a warning for the entire Himalayan region. “Kashmir should not wait for a Nepal-like catastrophe to understand the seriousness of what is happening in the Himalayas. We are witnessing increasing climate volatility, where prolonged dry periods can be followed by short-duration, extremely intense rainfall. In mountainous terrain, even a few minutes of extreme precipitation can trigger flash floods, landslides and debris flows,” Bhat said. He said the concern was not simply about whether Kashmir receives more or less rainfall. “The bigger concern is the changing character of rainfall and the increasing intensity of extreme events. A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, while warming can also contribute to instability of snow, ice and mountain slopes. Kashmir needs to prepare for compound disasters rather than treating every cloudburst as an isolated incident,” he said. Senior environmentalist Dr Tanveer Ahmad Khan said Kashmir’s vulnerability was being compounded by human pressure on an already fragile ecosystem. “Nepal is a warning, not merely a tragedy happening in another Himalayan country. Kashmir shares many of the same vulnerabilities—steep slopes, fragile geology, changing climate and increasing pressure from construction and infrastructure development. If drainage channels, river buffers, wetlands and unstable slopes continue to be disturbed, the impact of extreme weather will become much more severe,” Khan said. He said development planning had to take future climate risks into account. “We cannot continue to build as if the climate of the past is going to remain unchanged. Roads, hydropower projects, tourism infrastructure and settlements in mountain areas must be planned according to future climate risks. Every blocked natural drainage channel and every disturbed vulnerable slope reduces our margin of safety,” Khan added. The Nepal disaster has also underlined how quickly a single extreme event can cripple mountain infrastructure. Roads, bridges and power installations can be destroyed simultaneously, cutting off entire communities and making rescue operations far more difficult. For Kashmir, where highways, hydropower projects, tourism infrastructure and settlements are steadily expanding into mountain areas, experts say the lesson is particularly relevant. Afreen Khurshid, PhD research scholar at the University of Kashmir, said the focus must shift from responding to disasters to anticipating them. “The biggest lesson from Nepal is that vulnerability is created long before a disaster actually occurs. Climate change may intensify the hazard, but exposure and poor planning determine how devastating the final impact becomes. Kashmir urgently needs detailed hazard mapping of slopes, streams, flood channels and settlements, particularly in rapidly developing mountain areas,” she said. Khurshid stressed that early-warning systems must reach vulnerable communities on the ground. “An early warning is useful only when it reaches the last person living near a stream, a shepherd in the upper reaches, a tourist, a pilgrim or a person travelling through a vulnerable mountain corridor. Community preparedness, clearly identified evacuation routes and local response mechanisms can make the difference between an extreme weather event and a mass-casualty disaster,” she said.

stories.headline: It's Deeply Disappointing
stories.title: It's Deeply Disappointing
stories.summary: The decision to increase electricity tariffs in Jammu & Kashmir at a time when ordinary families are already struggling with the rising cost of living is deeply disappointing. More importantly, it raises a fundamental question of political accountability: what happened to the promises made to the people before the Assembly elections? The Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission has approved an average tariff increase of 6.83 per cent, applicable from September 1, 2026. For metered domestic consumers, the rate for consumption up to 200 units has increased from ₹2.30 to ₹2.45 per unit; for 201–400 units, from ₹4.00 to ₹4.20; and above 400 units, from ₹4.35 to ₹4.60 per unit. These figures may appear small when viewed from the comfort of government offices. For an ordinary household, however, every additional financial burden matters. From promise of relief to reality of higher bills The National Conference went before the electorate promising 200 units of free electricity. That promise naturally created expectations among families that desperately needed relief. Today, instead of experiencing the promised relief, consumers are confronting increased tariffs. The government may argue that its promise of free electricity and the general electricity tariff are technically separate matters. But politics cannot be reduced to technical explanations. The real question is what an ordinary voter understood when promises of cheaper or free electricity were made. People vote on the basis of promises and the reasonable expectations created by those promises. If financial constraints, distribution losses and the cost of purchasing electricity were realities after the election, they were realities before the election as well. Governments cannot discover economic realities only after obtaining the mandate of the people. Kashmir's winter cannot be viewed through ordinary consumption calculations The impact of electricity prices assumes an even greater significance in the Kashmir Valley. For people sitting outside Kashmir, electricity may be regarded primarily as a source of lighting and running household appliances. During Kashmir's severe winter, electricity is intimately connected with survival, warmth and basic human comfort. Temperatures fall below freezing in many areas. Water pipes freeze. Snowfall disrupts normal life. Families depend increasingly upon electric heaters, boilers, geysers, heating blankets and other appliances. The elderly, children and economically weaker families suffer the most. This means that electricity consumption during the harsh winter months cannot simply be treated as discretionary consumption. A Kashmiri family using additional electricity to keep its children or elderly parents warm is not indulging in luxury. It is responding to climatic necessity. And the timing is particularly unfortunate. The revised tariff becomes applicable from September 1 and will remain applicable through the approaching winter until March 31, 2027. The government should therefore ask itself a simple question: Is the period immediately preceding the harsh Kashmir winter the appropriate time to make electricity more expensive for households? Don't make consumers pay for inefficiency There is undoubtedly a financial problem in the electricity sector. Power has a cost. Distribution companies require revenue, and transmission and distribution losses have historically presented a serious challenge. But the solution cannot perpetually be to transfer the consequences of inefficiency onto honest consumers. The first responsibility of government should be to reduce losses, improve billing and collection, prevent electricity theft, modernise infrastructure and improve the efficiency of distribution companies. A family that pays its electricity bill regularly should not become the easiest source for balancing the books. Before asking consumers to pay more, the government must demonstrate what measurable reduction it has achieved in distribution losses and what administrative reforms it has undertaken to bring down costs. Efficiency must come before additional burden. The government's defence does not answer the political question Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has defended the increase by arguing that the government never promised that electricity tariffs would remain static and that power continues to be substantially subsidised. That may constitute an administrative defence. It does not answer the political question. The issue is not whether electricity continues to receive subsidy. The issue is whether the government is moving towards the relief that was promised to the electorate or away from it. The people were promised 200 units of free electricity. They are entitled to ask when that promise will translate into meaningful relief in their monthly household budgets. A government cannot seek political credit for promises and subsequently seek refuge behind regulatory calculations when people demand their implementation. BJP must stand with the consumer The Bharatiya Janata Party should unequivocally stand with the ordinary electricity consumer of Jammu & Kashmir. This is not an issue concerning Jammu or Kashmir alone. A shopkeeper in Jammu, a middle-class employee in Kathua, a farmer in the countryside, a pensioner in Srinagar and a family facing the freezing winter in north or south Kashmir all ultimately confront the same question: How much more can the household budget absorb? The BJP should demand that the Omar Abdullah government reconsider the tariff increase, particularly its impact upon domestic consumers, and immediately place before the people a transparent roadmap for fulfilling its electricity-related electoral commitments. Special consideration should also be given to the extraordinary electricity requirements of Kashmir during the winter months. If necessary, the government should explore a targeted winter electricity relief mechanism for vulnerable and middle-income domestic consumers in the Valley rather than allowing climatic necessity to translate into financial punishment. Promises carry a moral obligation Democracy does not end when votes are counted. An electoral promise creates a political and moral obligation. Governments must either implement their promises or candidly explain why they cannot do so. What they cannot reasonably do is promise relief while seeking votes and subsequently impose additional burdens after coming to power. The people of Jammu & Kashmir have endured decades of difficulties. They deserve governance that reduces their burdens rather than adding to them. The BJP must therefore raise its voice firmly, both inside and outside the Legislature, and demand: Withdraw or substantially reconsider the burden of the power tariff hike on domestic consumers. Protect Kashmir's households during the harsh winter. Reduce distribution losses before passing costs to consumers. And, above all, honour the commitments made to the people. Electricity in Jammu & Kashmir—particularly during a Kashmir winter—is not merely another commodity. For many families, it is warmth. It is security. It is a basic necessity of life. And a government elected on promises of relief should remember that before making that necessity more expensive. Author is an advocate and Chief Spokesperson of BJP in J&K
